one_line: Braintrust field CTO argues each agent architecture generation (single call, chain, ReAct loop, graph, product system) needs different evals, and that production traces should keep feeding the eval set.
summary: The speaker, Ameya Bhatawdekar (field CTO at Braintrust, auto-captioned as "Amir Bhattavdekar"), argues that AI systems are being re-platformed with each model generation, and that evals must change with the architecture. He walks through five stages: a single model call, a multi-step RAG chain, a ReAct-style loop, workflow graphs, and finally a product system with memory, sandboxes, and MCP/skills. Each stage adds failure surfaces that the previous eval style does not see. The loop era brought in run-to-run variance, so he recommends running each eval k times and reporting pass@k (capability) next to pass^k (reliability). He closes with a production flywheel: harvest traces, cluster failures (Braintrust's Topics feature), and turn new failure modes into eval cases. The talk is conceptual and vendor-framed, with almost no benchmark numbers.

key_ideas.idea: Architecture follows model updates, and evals have to follow the architecture.
key_ideas.detail: Old systems were built around model limits (for example weak tool calling). New models unlock capability only after re-architecture, and each new surface needs new evals. Evals are the durable asset that describes how the system should work.

key_ideas.idea: Each architecture generation fails in different places, so the eval unit changes.
key_ideas.detail: A single call needs a golden set scored on the final answer. A RAG chain needs per-step evals (parser, retrieval, context use, synthesis). Graphs need node-level evals plus tests for branching and retry logic.

key_ideas.idea: Loop agents need distribution-level evals, not single-run pass/fail.
key_ideas.detail: The same input can take different trajectories and still reach the right answer. Run each eval k times and look at the outcome distribution.

key_ideas.idea: Use pass@k for capability and pass^k for reliability.
key_ideas.detail: pass@k asks whether the agent succeeds at least once in k runs, which measures what it can do. pass^k asks how many of k runs succeed, which measures how dependable it is. A high pass@k with a low pass^k means the system works sometimes.

key_ideas.idea: Product-style agents have more failure surfaces than loop-level evals cover.
key_ideas.detail: Memory (within and across sessions), code-execution sandboxes, and MCP or skill directories add new failure points. Evals from the earlier generation give only partial coverage.

key_ideas.idea: Static evals go stale unless production data feeds back into them.
key_ideas.detail: Many teams describe a production-to-eval flywheel but do not run it. Harvest failures from production, including ones you already expected and ones you did not, and turn them into eval cases.

key_ideas.idea: Cluster production data to find failure modes nobody anticipated.
key_ideas.detail: Braintrust's Topics runs cluster analysis across production traces to surface new failure categories. Teams can then add guardrails or evals for those categories, not just more examples of known failures.

techniques.name: Architecture-matched eval suites
techniques.how: Match the eval design to the architecture: final-answer golden sets for a single call, per-step evals for chains, node/branch/retry evals for graphs, and k-run distribution evals for loops.
techniques.when: When you change the agent architecture or adopt a new model generation that changes how the system is built.

techniques.name: k-run pass@k and pass^k reporting
techniques.how: Run each eval case k times. Report pass@k as a capability measure and pass^k as a reliability measure.
techniques.when: For non-deterministic agent loops, where a single run gives a misleading signal.

techniques.name: Production failure clustering to harvest evals
techniques.how: Cluster production traces by failure type. Review the clusters, then add new eval cases and guardrails for failure modes that existing evals miss.
techniques.when: After shipping, or whenever the failure set is changing faster than your eval set.

techniques.name: Node-level and branch-level evals for graph workflows
techniques.how: Test each node's contract, branch selection, and retry loops separately, in addition to end-to-end runs.
techniques.when: When the agent is built as a workflow graph or state machine with hand-written branches.

numbers.claim: The talk gives no benchmark, cost, or latency figures. Its only concrete timing is a model release cadence of roughly every few months.
A single-prompt-plus-golden-set eval style was common about three years before the talk.
The ReAct loop became popular in late 2023 to early 2024.
Workflow graphs were popular in late 2024 to early 2025.
Tool calling and long-horizon planning improved noticeably in mid-to-late 2025, which made the ReAct loop viable again.

hot_takes: Architecture follows model updates, and evals have to follow the architecture.
Most teams that describe an eval flywheel do not actually run it, so their evals are static.
Reporting only pass@k hides unreliability. Pass^k is the number to watch for loop-based agents.

relevance.why: AgentOS has RAGAS evals and load tests but no distribution-level metric for agent runs. The pass@k vs pass^k split applies to the agent-facing layers (Crucible, SkillForge, EvolveCraft).
relevance.action: Add a k-run mode to the agent eval harness that reports pass@k and pass^k per case, starting with the MemoryMesh or Crucible task suite.

relevance.why: ProsHarness runs long Claude Code loops with checkpoint and resume. Reliability over repeated runs matters more than a single success, and the talk gives the metric for it.
relevance.action: Run one checkpointed ProsHarness workflow k times on the same spec and record pass^k before trusting loops or schedules.

relevance.why: Gives a clear framing for how eval design should follow architecture changes, which applies across the recurring interest in agent evals and context engineering.
relevance.action: Read Braintrust's Topics docs or the talk's flywheel section for the cluster-to-eval workflow, then compare it with the current eval plan.
